title: Testing & Debugging Your Own Code Live
summary: The end-of-round ritual of tracing test cases by hand and fixing bugs under time pressure, without a compiler to lean on.

slides.markdown:
"Looks right" is not the bar. It's the bar a candidate sets for themselves right before an interviewer finds the bug they didn't.

The last five to ten minutes of a round are usually spent testing, and how you test is graded as closely as how you coded — a candidate who traces their own logic by hand and finds their own off-by-one looks stronger than one with the same bug that a hint had to surface.

This topic covers picking test cases that actually stress the logic, dry-running code without a compiler, the bug classes that show up over and over, and what to do when you find a real bug with minutes left.

Declaring a solution finished the moment it compiles or reads correctly is the single biggest gap between how confident a candidate feels and how correct the code actually is. Code that looks obviously right to its own author is exactly where the author's blind spots live — you wrote it to match your mental model, so re-reading it mostly confirms your mental model, not the code's actual behavior.

Tracing an actual test case forces you to follow the code's real execution path instead of the path you intended, which is where off-by-ones, wrong loop bounds, and mishandled edge cases actually surface. Skipping this step to save time is a false economy — the time saved is smaller than the time lost if the bug is caught later, or not at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Picking test cases that stress the logic
slides.markdown:
Not all test cases are equally useful. A standing mental checklist that covers most bugs:

| Test case | What it exposes |
|---|---|
| Empty input | Crashes from assuming a first element exists |
| Single element | Loops or comparisons that assume at least two elements |
| Duplicates | Logic relying on uniqueness (sets, certain two-pointer setups) |
| Max size / boundary values | Off-by-one errors right at the array's edge |
| Already-sorted or reverse-sorted | Anything order-sensitive that assumes a mixed order |

Running through this list takes under a minute and catches the large majority of bugs candidates ship. Pick two or three rows that are most relevant to *this* problem rather than mechanically running all five every time.

On a shared doc or whiteboard, there's no compiler to catch a typo or run the code — you are the interpreter. The discipline: pick one concrete input, then execute your code **exactly as written**, line by line, updating variable values as you go, rather than mentally simulating what you *intended* the code to do.

The distinction matters because intent-simulation reproduces your own blind spots — if you meant `i < n` but wrote `i <= n`, mentally simulating "what I meant" never catches it, while literally executing the written line does. Write down variable states as you go (a small table of `left`, `right`, `sum` per iteration) rather than tracking it all in your head — externalizing state is what makes multi-step traces reliable under pressure.

A short list covers a disproportionate share of live bugs:

- **Off-by-one** — `<` vs `<=`, starting a loop at 0 vs 1, an inclusive vs exclusive boundary.
- **Mutation during iteration** — removing from a list while iterating over it, shifting indices out from under the loop.
- **Integer overflow** — rare in Python, real in Java/C++; multiplying two large ints or summing many values can silently wrap.
- **Off-by-reference** — mutating a shared object (a list passed by reference) when you meant to work on a copy.

Knowing this list means you can scan for these specific patterns during your trace instead of hoping a bug reveals itself generically.

slides.sectionTitle: A buggy loop and the trace that finds it
slides.markdown:
```python
def remove_evens(nums):
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[i] % 2 == 0:
            nums.pop(i)     # mutating the list mid-iteration
    return nums
```

Tracing `[2, 3, 4]` by hand, executed exactly as written:

- i=0: `nums[0]=2` is even → pop index 0 → list is now `[3, 4]`
- i=1: `nums[1]=4` (the list shifted left, so index 1 is now the old index 2) → even → pop → list is `[3]`
- i=2: out of range for a list of length 1 — loop ends early

Result: `[3]` — correct by luck here, but the trace exposes that `i` and the list's actual indices desynced after the first pop, which would silently skip elements on a different input like `[2, 4, 3]`. This is exactly the "mutation during iteration" bug class from §5, and only a literal trace — not a mental read-through — surfaces it.

slides.sectionTitle: Five minutes left, and you found a bug
slides.markdown:
Say what's wrong out loud immediately — don't fix silently and hope no one noticed there was ever a bug. "My trace shows this fails when there are duplicates, because the set is dropping the second occurrence I actually need to count" is valuable even before you've fixed it, because it proves the bug-finding process worked.

Then fix the **root cause**, not the symptom, even under time pressure — patching the specific failing case with a special-case `if` is a red flag interviewers watch for explicitly (see §8's pitfall). If time runs out before a full fix, stating the fix you'd make ("I'd change this to track counts instead of presence") is worth real credit even unimplemented, because it's still evidence of correct diagnosis.

The most common testing failure is running exactly one test case — usually the example from the prompt — declaring success, and stopping. The example case is chosen by the interviewer to be easy to read, not to be adversarial; passing it proves almost nothing about edge cases.

A closely related version: finding a bug and patching only the specific input that exposed it (adding an `if len(nums) == 0: return []` after a crash on empty input) without asking whether the same root cause breaks other inputs too. Both versions look like testing happened, while the actual coverage gained is minimal. The fix is the checklist in §3 — pick cases *designed* to stress the logic, not the one case that happened to be handed to you.

There's no fixed number of test cases that's "enough" — the goal is coverage of distinct failure modes, not volume. Two or three well-chosen cases (empty, a duplicate, a boundary value) that each exercise a different part of the logic beat five near-identical cases that all follow the happy path.

A practical stopping rule: keep testing until you've covered every branch your code actually has — every `if`, every loop's edge condition — at least once. Once every branch has been exercised by some trace, additional cases mostly re-confirm what you already know, and that time is better spent on a final complexity statement or answering the interviewer's questions.

This closing phase draws directly on [narrating your approach](narrating-your-approach) — saying what you're tracing and why, out loud, rather than tracing silently and only speaking once you find something.

For a longer worked set of traces and a broader edge-case checklist, see `data-structures-algorithms`'s [live-testing-discipline](live-testing-discipline) topic; and for how these same debugging instincts extend into a real production incident rather than an interview, see `engineering-craft`'s `debugging` group.
